validity.researcher_notes: This row's only citations (per wiki_citations.json) are two OPEC Annual Statistical Bulletin (ASB) editions. Both direct opec.org URLs are DEAD in the literal sense that fetching them returns the OPEC homepage, not the PDF (verified via curl -sIL: ASB2017 URL gives HTTP 301 -> https://www.opec.org, and the retry gives 403). This would ordinarily be a strong existence-flag candidate (GEM's own cited source doesn't actually resolve). However I located working Wayback Machine snapshots of BOTH editions and downloaded/ran pdftotext on each -- the pipeline is genuinely named and independently tabulated in official OPEC data, not a GEM-only entity: (1) OPEC ASB 2017 edition (web.archive.org snapshot, Table 9.9 'Main gas pipelines in OPEC Members, 2016', Libya section) lists 'Jakhira/Intisar (2) | Wintershall | 2 x 50 [miles] | 8, 20 [inches]' -- this matches GEM's Diameter='20, 8'in exactly (same two values), and 2 x 50 mi = 100 mi = 160.9 km matches GEM's LengthKnown=160.00 km almost exactly (GEM appears to have summed both parallel pipes' lengths, consistent with the source's own '(2)'/2x notation). (2) OPEC ASB 2012 edition (separate Wayback snapshot, Table 4.10 'Gas pipelines in OPEC Members, 2011', Libya section) independently lists 'Jakhira/Intesar | Wintershall | 80 [miles] | 20 [inches] | 2,407,250 [1,000 scm/yr]' -- i.e., in 2011 this was recorded as a single 20in/80mi line (a second, 8in line appears to have been added by the 2016 data year), and its Capacity column (2,407,250 thousand scm/yr = 2.407 bcm/yr) matches GEM's Capacity=2.40 bcm/y closely. The two editions show materially different numbers (80mi/single-pipe/20in vs 2x50mi/two-pipe/8+20in) confirming they are genuinely separate data-collection years, not one document copy-pasted -- real independent-in-time corroboration from the same institutional publisher (not treating this as fully cross-origin independent, since both are OPEC ASB). Route/endpoints also check out: Jakhira and Intisar/Intesar are both real, well-documented Sirte Basin oil/gas fields (Jakhira: discovered 1969, operated historically by Wintershall AG, operatorship transferred 29 Oct 2020 to Sarir Oil Operations, a JV of Wintershall Aktiengesellschaft (WIAG) and Libya's NOC -- confirmed via Wintershall Dea's own newsroom, which names Jakhira and 'Sirte Basin' directly, and via a live Jan-2024 Sarir Oil Operations tender for firefighting-system upgrades at the 'Jakhira station GOSP', confirming the field/station is still active and maintained as recently as 2024. Intisar is a separate, large, independently documented Sirte Basin field (Occidental discovery, 1967) per AAPG/GeoScienceWorld literature (paywalled, not citable here, but corroborates the endpoint is real, well outside GEM). CAVEAT: StartState/Province and EndState/Province are both recorded as 'Sirte Basin', which is a geological/informal region, not a Libyan administrative province (the field itself sits in Al Wahat district per Wintershall Dea's own description) -- minor precision issue, not flagging as a standalone concern since 'Sirte Basin' is a widely used and unambiguous descriptor for this cluster of pipelines (matches the roster's convention for sibling rows).

validity.researcher_notes: GEM records Owner1='BASF' 100%, with no ref (MISSING_REF). But GEM's own cited source names the operator as 'Wintershall' directly, never 'BASF': both the OPEC ASB 2017 edition (Table 9.9, 'Jakhira/Intisar (2) | Wintershall | 2 x 50 | 8, 20') and the 2012 edition (Table 4.10, 'Jakhira/Intesar | Wintershall | 80 | 20 | 2,407,250') list the owner/operator column as 'Wintershall'. BASF is Wintershall's historical parent (Wintershall AG was a wholly-owned BASF subsidiary before the 2019 DEA merger created Wintershall Dea, majority-owned by LetterOne/BASF) -- so 'BASF' is a defensible but imprecise parent-company simplification, and it is now further stale: Wintershall Dea's own newsroom (verified, independent of OPEC) confirms operatorship of these exact Sirte Basin fields (Jakhira/As Sarah, Area 91) was transferred on 29 October 2020 from WIAG to Sarir Oil Operations (SOO), a new joint venture between WIAG and Libya's National Oil Corporation -- a fact corroborated independently by a live Jan-2024 SOO tender referring to 'Jakhira station GOSP' as an SOO facility. So as of any data currency check in the last 5+ years, neither 'BASF' alone nor even 'Wintershall' alone fully reflects current operatorship; the JV (Sarir Oil Operations, WIAG+NOC) is the more accurate current operator/owner attribution.
